newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OASIS transmission system sees modest success.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OASIS transmission system sees modest success.

text.p: A week after its launch, users have rated the U.S. electricity industry's Open Access Same-time Information System (OASIS) a modest success despite reports of technical teething problems.

"The majority of the cases are fine. There are problems here and there," said Peter Hersh, project manager of grid operation and planning at Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), an industry group, in Palo Alto, Calif.
EPRI is overseeing the implementation of OASIS, which provides access to information on transmission prices and capacity to marketers and non-utility energy suppliers who do not own power lines.
The system, mandated by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, is considered a key step toward moving the country's electricity market toward open competition.
A variety of problems plagued the system. Technical troubles left frustrated users resorting to the old fashioned method of arranging transmission capacity over the telephone.
There are 22 major points or nodes on the Internet-based system, which generate the transmission data.
An OASIS node, operated by the Southwestern Power Pool (SPP), was one of the worst hit by technical problems.
"They were down for several days," Hersh said.

"It was hardware, software and database. It was a multitude of issues," said Nick Brown, SPP vice-president, The problems hampered a number of activities, including registering the roughly 400 users on its database, he said.
Since the system resumed operation, three-quarters of its users have been registered, Brown added.
SPP and system vendors tried to remedy the situation, even trying to improve the current design, he said.
"We're committed to put in a beefier server...We like what we have now. We want it to work better," Brown said.
Industry sources said they expect initial problems with OASIS would be short-term, with the system becoming easier to use as more people become familiar with it.
"For a project of this magnitude, it's working fairly well," Brown said.
